newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli shares finish sharply lower.
newsitem.headline: Israeli shares finish sharply lower.

text.p: Israeli shares closed sharply lower on Sunday as the market's correction was exacerbated by falling prices in New York last week and concerns about a government crisis, traders said.

The benchmark Mishtanim index of the top 100 shares fell 3.61 percent, or 8.68 points, to 231.91 on all-share turnover of 126 million shekels against 116 million shekels on Thursday, the last day of trading before the Israeli weekend.
The Maof 25 blue chip index closed 3.60 percent lower at 240.38.

"The long-awaited correction finally came. Now we have to see if it's only a correction or it's a trap," said a trader at Bank Hapoalim. "I believe that in the long run the trend is positive and 1997 will be a very good year for investors."
After posting sharp rises since the start of November, Mishtanim index has fallen in three out of the last four trading sessions. Today marked the biggest one-day decline.
"A consolidation period is healthy. The market gained 15 percent in three weeks without taking a rest. This is not normal," said Uri Schur at Eyal Securities.
"The question is whether or not the Maof will stabilise at around 225-230 or keep heading lower," Schur added.
Gad Hacker of Batucha Securites and Investments, attributed the decline to profit-taking, weakness on Wall Street and political uncertainty.

Other analysts, however, said the market was indifferent to the government's problems, which stem from allegations of high-level corruption in the appointment of an attorney-general earlier this month.

The state prosecutor said on Sunday that she would investigate charges that lawyer Roni Bar-On was named attorney-general after promisng to arrange a plea bargain for Aryeh Deri, leader of the Shas party. Bar-On was forced to resign shortly after his appointment.
"If there is a real government crisis the decline will continue," said Michael Weiss, of Evergreen Capital Markets. "But it is too early to sell...Everything is just on paper."
Other traders said the crisis had little impact on trading.
"The market was indifferent to the Deri crisis. Investors are showing little interest in the story. The decline was prompted by Wall Street's decline," Schur said.
"The Dow's decline was the main reason for today's decline. This is clearly seen by the fact that the main losers were arbitrage shares," the Hapoalim trader said.
Hacker noted that today's volume was low. "Sellers are not very aggressive. Prices are coming down, but volume is low," he said.

Analysts said the market would also be watching carefully the Bank of Israel's announcement on February interest rates after the close of trading on Monday. They said expectations were for a cut of 0.5 percentage point or less from the current 14.7 percent. Hacker said a 0.3 point cut looked realsistic.
Weiss said a reduction of more than 0.5 point would give the market a boost, even with continued political concerns. He said such a cut was possible.
"The papers say that there is a lot of pressure on the governor (Jacob Frenkel) to reduce rates," he said.

The most active shares were Israel Chemicals, which fell 3.0 percent to 341 agorot on turnover of 9.6 million shekels; Koor Industries, which plunged 5.0 percent to 31,352 agorot on volume of 6.8 million shekels; and Teva Pharmaceutical Industries, which dropped 3.75 percent to 1,806 agorot on volume of five million shekels.
($1 = 3.30 shekels)
- Dan Gerstenfeld, Tel Aviv newsroom, 972-3-537-2211
